lead: A centroid is the point where a shape would balance. For a rectangle or a circle it sits at a known place. For a shape bounded by an arbitrary curve, the average of all the small elements becomes an integral, and you integrate x dA and y dA over the area. For a shape built from rectangles, circles and triangles, the same average is taken row by row in a table. The two methods are one idea: a weighted average of positions, weighted by area, length or volume.
prereq: You need 4.1 for the centroid definition and the first moment of area, and first-year integration of polynomials.

sections.h3: Integration: one strip at a time

blocks.text: A shape bounded by a curve has no single width and height, so you cut it into thin strips. Take a vertical strip of width dx at position x, running from the x-axis up to the curve y = f(x). The strip is a thin rectangle: its area is dA = y dx and it balances at half its height, so its centroid is at (x, y/2).
x̄ = ∫ x dA / ∫ dA = ∫ x y dx / ∫ y dx
blocks.where: x is the horizontal position of the strip in mm; y is the curve height in mm; dA = y dx is the strip area in mm²; the integral runs between the left and right ends of the area.

blocks.text: ȳ = ∫ (y/2) dA / ∫ dA = ∫ (y²/2) dx / ∫ y dx
blocks.where: ȳ is the height of the centroid in mm; y²/2 comes from (height y) × (centroid height y/2).

items: Sketch the area and mark the x and y axes.
Choose vertical strips when y = f(x) is one curve; choose horizontal strips when x = g(y) is simpler.
Write dA and the strip centroid: (x, y/2) for vertical, (x/2, y) for horizontal.
Integrate numerator and denominator between the limits.
Divide to get x̄ and ȳ; round to three significant figures.

blocks.text: If the area lies between two curves y₁ and y₂, the strip height is y₂ − y₁ and its centroid is at (y₁ + y₂)/2. Double integration is the same idea in two directions: x̄ = ∫∫ x dy dx / ∫∫ dy dx; use it only when a single strip would have to be split.

blocks.where: L is the length of a plane curve in mm; ds = √(dx² + dy²) is a small piece of the curve. Then x̄ = ∫ x ds / L and ȳ = ∫ y ds / L.

sections.h3: Composite areas: the same average as a table

blocks.text: A composite area is built from standard pieces — rectangles, triangles, circles — whose centroids you already know from 4.1. The centroid of the whole is the area-weighted average of the piece centroids:
x̄ = Σ Aᵢ x̄ᵢ / Σ Aᵢ, ȳ = Σ Aᵢ ȳᵢ / Σ Aᵢ
blocks.where: Aᵢ is the area of piece i in mm²; x̄ᵢ and ȳᵢ are its centroid coordinates in mm, all measured from the same pair of reference axes.

blocks.text: Make a table with one row per piece: label, A, x̄, ȳ, A x̄, A ȳ. Enter a hole as a negative area; its centroid coordinates stay positive. Add each column, then divide. The total row gives the answer. The reference lines must be the same for every row — write them on the sketch before you start.
Composite lines use length in place of area: x̄ = Σ Lᵢ x̄ᵢ / Σ Lᵢ. A bent wire of a straight part and a semicircular arc is two rows; the straight part's centroid is at its midpoint.
A composite volume uses volume in place of area. For a solid made of a cylinder, a cone and a block, list each part's volume Vᵢ and centroid x̄ᵢ, ȳᵢ, z̄ᵢ, then:
x̄ = Σ Vᵢ x̄ᵢ / Σ Vᵢ
blocks.where: Vᵢ is the volume of part i in mm³; x̄ᵢ is its centroid coordinate in mm; the sum runs over all parts. Use the same formula for ȳ and z̄.

blocks.text: By integration, a volume is cut into thin discs or slices: dV = A(y) dy for a disc of area A at height y, with centroid at the disc centre. Keep every length in millimetres before multiplying; mm × mm × mm gives mm³, but mixing mm and cm gives a wrong total.

figure.caption: The table for the T-section: the web and flange rows give area, centroid height and area times centroid. The total row's 67.8 mm is the answer; every height is measured from the bottom of the web.

spec.title: T-section table: A in mm², ȳ in mm, Aȳ in 10³ mm³
spec.aria: A composite table for a T-section lists the web and the flange with their areas, centroid heights and area times centroid, and the total row gives the answer 67.8 mm.

examples.question: A T-section has a web 20 mm wide and 80 mm tall, and a flange 100 mm wide and 20 mm thick on top of the web. Find the centroid. Take y upward from the bottom of the web and x from the left edge of the 100 mm flange.
steps: Take y from the bottom of the web and x from the left edge of the 100 mm flange. The section is symmetric about the vertical centre line, so x̄ = 50 mm by inspection; the flange is 100 mm wide and the web is centred on it.
Web: width 20 mm, height 80 mm. A₁ = 20 × 80 = 1600 mm². Its centroid is at half its height: ȳ₁ = 80/2 = 40 mm.
Flange: width 100 mm, thickness 20 mm, sitting on top of the web. A₂ = 100 × 20 = 2000 mm². Its centroid is 80 mm (web height) + 20/2 mm = 90 mm above the base.
First moments: A₁ȳ₁ = 1600 × 40 = 64000 mm³. A₂ȳ₂ = 2000 × 90 = 180000 mm³. Sum = 244000 mm³.
ȳ = ΣAȳ / ΣA = 244000 / 3600 = 67.777... mm = 67.8 mm above the base.
examples.answer: The centroid is 67.8 mm above the bottom of the web, on the vertical centre line (x̄ = 50 mm from the left edge of the flange).
examples.check:
A1 = 20 * 80
y1 = 40
A2 = 100 * 20
y2 = 90
A = A1 + A2
ybar = (A1*y1 + A2*y2) / A
xbar = 50.0
print(f"{ybar:.1f}")
print(f"{xbar:.1f}")

traps: Taking the centroid height of a rectangle as its full height instead of half of it.
Measuring x̄ and ȳ from different reference lines for different rows of the table.
Forgetting that a hole is a negative area but its centroid coordinates are still positive distances from the reference lines.
Mixing mm and cm in the same table; convert first, then multiply.
Using the composite table for a shape whose parts overlap; split the shape into non-overlapping pieces.

quiz.q: State the formula for ȳ of an area using vertical strips under y = f(x).
quiz.a: ȳ = ∫ (y²/2) dx / ∫ y dx, because each strip has area y dx and centroid height y/2.

quiz.q: Why is the centroid of a thin vertical strip at y/2 and not at y?
quiz.a: The strip is a thin rectangle of uniform width. A rectangle balances at its mid-height, so its centroid is halfway between its bottom and top.

quiz.q: A composite area has two parts: A₁ = 400 mm² at x̄₁ = 20 mm and A₂ = 600 mm² at x̄₂ = 80 mm. Find x̄ to three significant figures.
A rectangle is 60 mm wide and 30 mm tall. A circular hole of radius 10 mm is cut with its centre 15 mm above the base. Find ȳ of the net area.
quiz.a: Rectangle A = 1800 mm², ȳ = 15 mm, Aȳ = 27000 mm³. Hole A = π×10² = 314.2 mm², ȳ = 15 mm, Aȳ = 4712 mm³ (negative). Net A = 1485.8 mm², net ΣAȳ = 22288 mm³, ȳ = 22288/1485.8 = 15.0 mm. Both centroids are at the same height, so the hole does not move ȳ.

quiz.q: A student gets ȳ = 40 mm for the T-section in the worked example. Which mistake most likely produced this value?
quiz.a: Using only the web row: 64000/1600 = 40 mm. The student ignored the flange, which has a larger area and a higher centroid, so the true ȳ is 67.8 mm.

quiz.q: For a semicircular wire of radius R closed by its diameter, which table row would you enter as negative, and why?
quiz.a: No row is negative. The semicircular arc has length πR and centroid height 2R/π; the diameter has length 2R and centroid height 0. Both are positive lengths. Only holes or cut-outs are negative, and a closing line is not a hole.

quiz.q: Write the table formula for x̄ of a composite line made of parts of length Lᵢ.
quiz.a: x̄ = Σ Lᵢ x̄ᵢ / Σ Lᵢ.

quiz.q: When is a horizontal strip better than a vertical strip?
quiz.a: When the boundary is easier to write as x = g(y). Then a horizontal strip of height dy has dA = x dy and centroid at (x/2, y), and one integral covers the area instead of two.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the composite table is the hand method behind CAD mass properties: every solid model is a mesh of small volumes, and the same ΣVx̄/ΣV runs over millions of elements. Search for "centroid of a polygon" (the shoelace formula) and "mass properties of a mesh". The integral form becomes a numerical quadrature when the boundary is a spline. Offshore and aerospace weight budgets use exactly this table to keep the centre of gravity inside a safe envelope.
